text:
Every job ran last night, and every one reported success. At six, the dashboard still shows yesterday's numbers. Nothing failed. Nothing was ready, either. This round is keeping data on time: tasks in order, recovery from failure, and bad data caught early. Fourteen questions: eleven with a figure, then three quick ones.

Question one. What does an orchestrator give you over cron? Cron, the Unix job scheduler, starts a command at a set time, and nothing more. Schedule extract at one and transform at two. The night extract runs long, transform starts anyway, on half the data. An orchestrator runs a DAG, a directed acyclic graph: tasks joined by their dependencies, so each starts only after its upstream tasks succeed. On top come retries, backfills, monitoring and lineage. Airflow, Dagster and Prefect, three open-source orchestrators, keep the graph and every run's history. Cron keeps neither.

Question two. How does Dagster model pipelines differently from Airflow? Airflow is task-centric: you write the steps to run, and wire them in order. Dagster is asset-centric: you declare the data each function produces, a table or a file, and Dagster works out the graph from what each one reads. So lineage and freshness come built in: every asset knows what produced it, and when. It also has stronger typing and testing primitives.
